body:
Why communication is a defence technology

Modern defence systems depend on the movement of reliable information. Aircraft, ships, vehicles and personnel may observe the same situation from different locations. Communication systems help them share reports and maintain an agreed understanding of relevant conditions.

A communication system has a sender, a message, a transmission medium and a receiver. The message may be spoken information, written data, an image or a sensor report. Reliability depends on the equipment, the environment and the correctness of the information transmitted.

Wired and wireless communications

MethodHow information travelsImportant limitation
Wired electrical linkElectrical signals through a conductorRequires a physical connection
Optical fibreLight signals through an optical mediumRequires an installed fibre path
Radio communicationElectromagnetic waves through spaceAffected by propagation conditions and interference
Satellite communicationRadio links through a satelliteDepends on satellite access, equipment and link conditions

Radio communication may operate over a line-of-sight path, where the communicating points have a suitable unobstructed radio path. Terrain and obstacles can affect such links. Satellite communication can extend communication beyond some terrestrial limitations, but it does not remove every constraint on availability or reliability.

Security, accuracy and redundancy

Military communication must protect sensitive information. Encryption transforms information so that it is not readily understandable to an unauthorised person who intercepts it. However, encryption alone cannot establish that the original information was factually correct.

Authentication helps establish that information or a communicating party comes from an expected source. Redundancy means providing alternative equipment or communication paths so that a single failure need not stop the entire information flow.

A false report can remain false even when transmitted securely. Commanders therefore need both protected communications and reliable observation.

What battlefield digitisation means

Battlefield digitisation means using digital sensors, communications, data processing and displays to collect, combine and present relevant battlefield information for human decision-making.

Examples include digital maps, vehicle-position information, UAV imagery, ground-surveillance sensors and electronic reports. Their value depends on how accurately the information is collected and whether it reaches the people who need it.

From individual sensors to a common picture

A ground sensor may detect an object, while an aircraft observes the same area from above. If both observations are separately displayed without comparison, the system may count one object twice. Data fusion compares observations, checks their reliability and combines them into a more useful common picture.

A common surveillance picture is a shared representation of relevant observations from several sources. It helps people understand the same situation, but it is not a guarantee that every object has been correctly identified.

Indian example: SANJAY Battlefield Surveillance System

On 24 January 2025, the Ministry of Defence announced the flagging-off of SANJAY – The Battlefield Surveillance System (BSS).

The system integrates information from ground and aerial battlefield sensors, checks the information, reduces duplication and produces a common surveillance picture. It uses the Army's secured data network and satellite communication network to provide information for decision support.

SANJAY is therefore best identified as a battlefield surveillance and information-fusion system, not as a tank, an artillery gun or a UAV. Its role illustrates the connection between communications technology and the wider land-defence system.

Connecting air, naval and land systems

The 3 major environments use different platforms and sensors, but they follow related principles:

  • Air: Aircraft and UAVs depend on aerodynamics, propulsion, navigation, communications and airworthiness.
  • Sea: Warships and submarines depend on propulsion, navigation, underwater acoustics and maritime information.
  • Land: Tanks, infantry vehicles and artillery depend on mobility, protection, weapons, sensors and secure communications.

All 3 environments benefit from correctly identified information. A surveillance sensor is not the same as a weapon, and an information display cannot replace verification or human judgement.

Prelims focus

  • Radio and satellite communication use electromagnetic waves; optical fibre carries information through light.
  • Encryption protects information from unauthorised reading but does not guarantee factual correctness.
  • Data fusion combines and checks observations from multiple sources.
  • SANJAY is the Battlefield Surveillance System and was flagged off on 24 January 2025.
  • SANJAY integrates ground and aerial sensor inputs into a common surveillance picture.
  • Trap: SANJAY is a surveillance and information system, not a weapons platform.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 6, Ch. 12, 'Electricity and Circuits'; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Ch. 12, 'Electricity', and Ch. 13, 'Magnetic Effects of Electric Current'; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Defence, 'Raksha Mantri flags-off SANJAY – The Battlefield Surveillance System from New Delhi', 24 January 2025; consulted 14 November 2026. Dated programme information in this lesson has a content cutoff of 14 November 2026.]
